capex_override.ack_reason: The band check anchors on the last filed value under an engine-read tag, which is the FY2024 PaymentsForConstructionInProcess fact of -$17,170,000 — a construction-payables change filed with a negative sign (statements.json flags it as a sign slip), not the filer's recurring capex line at all. On absolute value the override ($59,288,000) is 3.45x that anchor, inside the 0.1x-10x band, and the engine marks it in-band; this acknowledgment is carried anyway because the anchor is not a capex figure. The override is not an estimate lacking an anchor — it is the median of the filer's own FY2023-25 PaymentsForCapitalImprovements figures from its FY2025 10-K.
capex_override.reason: DATA_GAP:capex — capex missing for FY2025 under every candidate tag the engine reads, because in the FY2025 10-K EastGroup stopped filing PaymentsForConstructionInProcess (the minor tag the engine read for FY2022-24, whose FY2024 fact is a signed construction-payables change of -$17,170,000, not capex). The filer's recurring real-estate capex is the cash-flow line 'Capital improvements' (us-gaap PaymentsForCapitalImprovements), which statements.py reads as the capex series ($51,116,000 FY2023 / $59,288,000 FY2024 / $75,830,000 FY2025) but which is not in the engine's candidate tag list — the same dead end documented for MAA, AMH, ELS and others in this sweep. The engine applies this single value to every missing period (FY2025 and the assumed-zero years); filed values are never replaced, so FY2023 ($12,163,000) and FY2024 (-$17,170,000) in the base window still carry the wrong minor tag — disclosed, not hidden: the median of the three window years under the fill is the corrected FY2025 year, so the normalized base is the corrected figure (see analysis.md). Against the true per-year capital-improvements figures the single value overstates FY2025 capex charge by $0 in the median construction (it IS the FY2024 figure) and understates FY2025's filed $75,830,000 by $16,542,000 (flatters the latest year — stated here; the TTM pin charges the same $59,288,000, also below the FY2025 run rate, so the base is if anything generous on capex). Excluded, deliberately: 'Development of real estate' ($321,934,000 FY2025) and 'Acquisition of real estate' ($143,099,000 FY2025) are growth investment presented separately by the filer; charging them as capex would double-count growth the portfolio expansion already paid for (same treatment as AMH/AHR in this sweep).
capex_override.source: Form 10-K for fiscal year ended December 31, 2025 (filed 2026-02-11, accession 0000049600-26-000010), Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, investing activities line 'Capital improvements' (us-gaap PaymentsForCapitalImprovements): $(51,116) thousand for FY2023, $(59,288) thousand for FY2024 and $(75,830) thousand for FY2025; the override value is the median of the three filed years (the FY2024 figure). Cross-checked against statements.json, whose capex series is exactly this line.

moat_against: Real estate is replicable with capital — no network effects; tenant lock-in is a multi-year lease, and shallow-bay space competes with new build-for-rent industrial supply

Filed returns are moderate, not wide-moat: ROE 9.5% (FY2022) → 7.7% (FY2023) → 6.9% (FY2024) → 7.4% (FY2025) in fundamentals.json; roic_proxy and gross margin are not computable from the filed REIT presentation — no record of returns durably well above the cost of capital
Growth is equity-funded: share count CAGR 7.3%/yr, issuance proceeds $692,312,000 (FY2023), $717,659,000 (FY2024), $264,071,000 (FY2025) — per-share economics lag portfolio growth

Sun Belt concentration (Florida, Texas, Arizona, California) and a post-COVID industrial supply wave in several markets cap rent growth as the 34% leasing spreads normalize; same-property NOI guidance (+6.8% for 2026) is already below the +8.8% YTD print
Development is cyclical: the $487M pipeline (17 projects, 3.2M sq ft) must lease up through whatever demand does next; development starts guidance was cut one quarter and raised the next in 2026
moat_for: Infill shallow-bay locations in supply-constrained Sun Belt markets: zoning/permit friction and scarce infill land make the 65.8M sq ft portfolio hard to replicate at any price near book; quarter-end occupancy 95.6%, same-store 96.9% (Q2 2026)
Demonstrated pricing power: Q2 2026 leasing spreads +34% GAAP / +19% cash on a record 3.9M sq ft signed; cash same-store NOI +8.3% in Q2, +8.8% YTD

Development alpha: self-developed projects transfer at a ~9.4% stabilized yield (management, Q2 2026 coverage), well above acquisition cap rates — a structural cost advantage over REITs that must buy growth
Balance sheet as a competitive weapon: debt/total market cap 12.9%, debt/EBITDA 3.0x, coverage 15.1x, no revolver drawn ($675M available) at Q2 2026 — cheap, always-available capital through cycles
Diversified rent roll (top 10 tenants 6.6% of rents) and 186 consecutive quarterly dividends; FFO/share compounded ~10.7%/yr over five years (peer coverage)
moat_justification: Moderate/narrow 5/10: infill shallow-bay scarcity in Sun Belt markets, demonstrated rent pricing power (leasing spreads +34% GAAP / +19% cash, cash same-store NOI +8-9%) and a development channel that creates assets at a ~9.4% stabilized yield give EastGroup more than a generic landlord's moat, but the assets remain replicable with capital, there is no lock-in beyond leases, growth is bought with continuous equity issuance (shares +7.3%/yr), and filed ROE has run only 6.9-7.7% in the last three years with roic_proxy not computable from the REIT presentation — not the sustained well-above-cost-of-capital record a 7+ requires. In line with KIM (5) and above the generic REIT 4s (AMH, AHR, MAA, INVH) on the strength of the development alpha and spreads.
